passage:
Okay, so this was last term, in our class chat. Devika sent a long message about her science project, and it had one spelling mistake. Then a row of laughing faces started. Six, seven of them. Somebody wrote "typo queen".
I'm Urmila, and I read every reply and typed nothing. My thumb hovered. I thought, if I say something they will turn on me. So I put the phone down and ate my lunch, and my rice tasted of nothing.
That evening I messaged Devika alone: "That chat was unkind. I'm sorry I stayed quiet. Your project sounds great." She wrote back, "Thank you for saying that."

qa.q: How many laughing faces did the class chat show after Devika's message?
qa.a: A row of laughing faces started, six or seven of them.

qa.q: Why did Urmila type nothing while the laughing faces piled up?
qa.a: Urmila was afraid that the others would turn on her too. The hovering thumb and the tasteless lunch show she felt uneasy and guilty about staying quiet.

qa.q: What did Urmila do that evening, and what else could a bystander try in the chat itself?
qa.a: Urmila messaged Devika privately to say the chat was unkind and to apologise for staying quiet. In the chat a bystander could also change the subject or ask a plain question about the project.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when the laughing faces began and later when Urmila wrote privately?
qa.a: Devika probably felt embarrassed and small at first, and then a little comforted by Urmila's private message. Saying "Thank you" shows the kindness reached her.

grounding: A student watches classmates mock a member's message with laughing faces and stays silent in the chat, then offers private support.

passage:
I sit behind Nilesh in class, and I saw him on Friday during free period. Someone posted a screenshot of Ritika's message in our class chat, and laughing faces started stacking up under it. I could see Nilesh's screen over his shoulder. He read it, very still, and did not add a face.
Then Nilesh typed, "Did anyone get the maths sheet for Monday?" Two people answered. The faces stopped.
After the bell, Nilesh walked to Ritika's desk and said something quiet. Ritika nodded. I don't know what he was feeling, but he looked uncomfortable all the way home.
— Gargi

qa.q: What did Nilesh type to the class chat after reading the screenshot?
qa.a: Nilesh typed, "Did anyone get the maths sheet for Monday?"

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling while sitting very still and not adding a face?
qa.a: Nilesh seems to have been uneasy and unwilling to join in. Gargi cannot know for sure, but the stillness and the uncomfortable look on the way home suggest it.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that helped Ritika, and why did it work?
qa.a: Nilesh changed the topic to the maths sheet, so people had something else to answer and the faces stopped. Then Nilesh spoke quietly to Ritika at the desk after the bell.

qa.q: What might Ritika have felt when Nilesh came to the desk after the bell?
qa.a: Ritika may have felt relieved and less alone, since the nod suggests the quiet words were welcome. Being singled out in the chat is painful, so a private kindness matters.

grounding: A student watches classmates mock a member's message, does not join in, changes the topic and offers private support, as seen by someone sitting behind.

passage:
Monday. Kunal posted a line from his English poem in the class chat, asking if the ending worked. Within a minute there were rows of laughing faces, then "Shakespeare returns," then a sticker of a crying clown. Anjali saw it all on the bus. Her thumb hovered. She put the phone in her bag.
Tuesday. Kunal didn't come to school. The chat kept going: someone had turned his line into a joke song. Anjali felt sick every time it buzzed, and a bit guilty for smiling at the first joke.
Friday. It started again, this time about Kunal's haircut. Anjali typed quickly: "Has anyone done Q3 of the maths sheet? I'm stuck." Two people answered. The jokes stopped.
Then she messaged Kunal privately: "I liked your ending. Truly. Want to walk to tuition together?"
He replied after a while: "Yes please. Thanks."

qa.q: What did Anjali type in the group chat on Friday?
qa.a: Anjali typed, "Has anyone done Q3 of the maths sheet? I'm stuck."

qa.q: How did Anjali feel on Tuesday when the chat kept going?
qa.a: Anjali felt sick and guilty, uneasy each time it buzzed and ashamed of smiling at the first joke.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Changing the topic with a real question stopped the jokes without a fight, and the private message gave Kunal support he could feel.

qa.q: What was the week like for Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal likely felt humiliated and alone, missing school on Tuesday, and grateful when someone finally reached out.

grounding: A student watches classmates mock another's message and stays silent, then changes the topic and offers private support.

passage:
"Nikita, you were quiet in the car. Is it the class group again? Let me tell you something from when I was fifteen," said Kunal Chacha.
"We had just got our first group chat, the whole class. A girl called Farzana sent a message with a spelling mistake. 'Congragulations,' she wrote, to our cricket captain. Someone sent a laughing face. Then ten. Then jokes about her English.
"I saw every one. I didn't laugh, but I didn't say anything either. I told myself it wasn't my business.
"Next day she didn't come. She changed sections the next month.
"Years later I met her at a wedding. She said, 'You were the one who never laughed. I wished you had said something.'
"One line would have done, Nikita. 'Enough, yaar.' Or a message just to her: 'Ignore them.' I've carried that silence longer than she's carried the jokes, I think.

qa.q: What word did Farzana misspell?
qa.a: Farzana wrote "Congragulations" to the cricket captain.

qa.q: What was young Kunal feeling while he watched the jokes?
qa.a: Young Kunal felt uncomfortable and uneasy, not laughing, but talking himself into silence by saying it wasn't his business.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could have changed things?
qa.a: When the laughing faces began, young Kunal could have posted "Enough, yaar" or privately messaged Farzana to ignore them, which might have slowed the pile-on and left her less alone.

qa.q: How did Farzana experience the pile-on?
qa.a: Farzana felt humiliated enough to stay away and change sections, and she felt let down that the boy who never laughed also never spoke up.

grounding: An elder recalls watching classmates mock a message and staying silent, showing how bystander silence lets a pile-on grow.

passage:
Abhinav was squeezed into the back seat of the Aizawl school bus, revising chemistry for the next day's test, when the class chat lit up. Lalremsiami had suggested the class do a clean-up drive instead of the usual picnic. The replies came fast: laughing faces, "Miss Environment," a picture of a broom with her name on it.
Abhinav watched. He thought her idea was good. But the bus was bumping, the test was tomorrow, and speaking up felt like painting a target on himself. He scrolled past.
Twenty more messages. Lalremsiami had gone quiet.
At the next stop, he stopped scrolling. He typed in the group: "Has anyone got the notes for chapter 4? Test tomorrow." The chat turned to notes.
Then, privately: "Your clean-up idea is better than a picnic. I'd join."
A minute later: "Thank you. I felt so stupid."

qa.q: What had Lalremsiami suggested to the class?
qa.a: Lalremsiami suggested the class do a clean-up drive instead of the usual picnic.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav scroll past at first?
qa.a: He was nervous that speaking up would paint a target on himself, and he was stressed about the next day's test.

qa.q: What small steps did Abhinav take that helped?
qa.a: He changed the topic in the group by asking for chapter 4 notes and sent Lalremsiami a private message backing her idea.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami when the replies came in?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt stupid and humiliated as the jokes piled up, and she felt grateful and relieved when Abhinav wrote to her privately 🤍

grounding: A student watches classmates mock another's message and is silent at first, then changes the topic and offers private support.

passage: Madhuri was halfway through her maths homework in her Shillong flat when the class group lit up. Lalremsiami had posted: "Does anyone know if the bio prakticle is tomorrow or Friday? I missed the notice." Within seconds Rohan quoted it with "prakticle??", and a stream of laughing faces followed. Nine, ten, eleven reactions. Someone added a sticker of a confused cartoon cow. Madhuri's thumb hovered. She remembered Lalremsiami lending her a pen in the exam hall without being asked. She put the phone face down, then picked it up again. The laughing kept stacking up, and Lalremsiami had gone quiet. Madhuri typed in the group: "Practical is Friday, notice is on page 2 of the portal. Also has anyone started Q7?" The chat swung to Q7. Then she messaged Lalremsiami privately: "that wasn't funny. you ok?" A minute later: "yeah. thanks for answering the actual question 🙏"

qa.q: Which day is the practical?
qa.a: Practical is Friday.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as her thumb hovered over the phone?
qa.a: Madhuri felt uneasy and torn, remembering Lalremsiami's kindness but hesitant to stand against a laughing group.

qa.q: Which two moves helped, and why?
qa.a: Answering the real question and asking about Q7 changed the topic so the pile-on stopped, and the private "you ok?" told Lalremsiami someone was on her side.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami while the laughing faces stacked up?
qa.a: She had asked a real question and got mocked for a spelling slip, so she went quiet, likely embarrassed and alone until someone answered her.

grounding: Shows a student watching classmates mock a member's message with laughing reactions, first staying silent and then changing the topic and offering private support.
